item.title: Cancer-associated fibroblasts as architects of tumor immune geography and lymphoid organization
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79106-3

Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are a heterogeneous population of stromal cells that participate in the formation of tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs). Here, the authors review the current knowledge on how CAF subsets shape the organization and function of immune cells within TLS and discuss the clinical implications of these CAF-TLS interactions.

item.title: The transcriptional regulator IκBζ is essential for ILC2 effector functions
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78876-0

Group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2) are important for the anti-helminth immune response. Here the authors show that the effector program of ILC2s depends on transcriptional regulation of the alarmins IL-25 and IL-33 by IκBζ, leading to efficient hookworm clearance in a mouse model.
item.dc:title: The transcriptional regulator IκBζ is essential for ILC2 effector functions

item.title: Evidence and measures of the digital usage divide from 40 million Windows devices
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78689-1

Using usage data from 40 million Windows devices, this paper develops measures of digital engagement in the USA, revealing digital inequalities that are not captured by traditional measures of internet access alone.

item.title: SimPoly: Simulation of polymers with machine learning force fields derived from first principles
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78736-x

The authors develop a machine learning force field trained only on quantum-chemical data that can reproduce measured key polymer properties such as densities and glass transition temperatures.

item.title: Archival and palaeoenvironmental documentation of extreme climate events reveals generational amnesia in collective memory
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78922-x

Collective memory shapes how societies respond to climate extremes, but its long-term biases are hard to observe. Here, the authors show that historical severity assessments of droughts and floods in northern China over 430 years are biased toward recent experience, consistent with an agent-based model of generational amnesia.
item.dc:title: Archival and palaeoenvironmental documentation of extreme climate events reveals generational amnesia in collective memory
